OAuth 2.0 lets your app securely access Zoom APIs for users or accounts. Zoom supports industry-standard OAuth 2.0 ( [rfc6749](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749)) flows to handle authorization and access tokens.

Your app can request, refresh, and revoke tokens based on its type and authorization method. Tokens expire after a set time and may need renewal or refresh.

**Note**

Zoom API library for Rivet handles OAuth for you. For more information, go to [Zoom Rivet](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/rivet/) → **Javascript** → **Get started** → **Initialize the client**.

## Request an access token [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#request-an-access-token)

Zoom offers OAuth 2.0 flows and grant types for these four authorization use cases.

Account authorization

User authorization

Device authorization

Client authorization

### App Type: [Server to Server](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/internal-apps/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-server-to-server)

Get an `access_token` to call APIs for your own Zoom account.

To request an access token, send a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/token`. Include a basic authorization header and provide the following required parameters either as query parameters or in the request body using the `x-www-form-urlencoded` format.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `account_credentials` |
| `account_id` | Your Zoom account ID, found on the Server to Server app build page. |

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

### Example request [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#example-request)

Copy

9

1

›

POST https://zoom.us/oauth/token?grant\_type=account\_credentials&account\_id=Wk9PTV9BQ0NPVU5UX0lE

Request headers

Copy

9

1

2

3

›

{

"Authorization":"Basic Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfSUQ6Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfU0VDUkVU"

}

If successful, the response body is a JSON representation of the `access_token`.

Copy

9

1

2

3

4

5

6

7

›

{

"access\_token":"<JWT\_TOKEN>",

"token\_type":"bearer",

"expires\_in":3600,

"scope":"user:read:user:admin",

"api\_url":"https://api.zoom.us"

}

Access tokens expire after one hour. After your access token expires, you can request a new one. Zoom does not require a separate refresh flow.

### App Type: [General](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-general)

Get an `access_token` to call APIs on behalf of a Zoom user or Zoom account.

#### Get a user authorization code [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#get-a-user-authorization-code)

You can get a user authorization code by adding your app to your Zoom account. To do this, navigate to the **Local Test** page, and choose **Add App Now**.

Alternatively, construct the authorization URL using the following format:

Copy

9

1

›

https://zoom.us/oauth/authorize?response\_type=code&client\_id=ZOOM\_CLIENT\_ID&redirect\_uri=REDIRECT\_URI

See [section 4.1.1 of _The OAuth 2.0 Authorization Framework RFC_](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-4.1.1) for details.

#### User authorization flow [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#user-authorization-flow)

1. When the user visits this URL, Zoom prompts them to sign in (if not already signed in) and to grant the requested permissions.
2. After the user authorizes the app, Zoom redirects the user’s browser to the specified `redirect_uri` and includes an authorization code. For example, `https://example.com/callback?code=AUTH_CODE`.
3. Your application should capture this authorization code from the redirect request and exchange it for an `access_token` using the OAuth token endpoint.
4. If this is the user's first time authorizing your app, or if you've updated scopes or webhook settings, Zoom will prompt the user to authorize again before issuing a new authorization code.

#### Exchange authorization code for access token [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#exchange-authorization-code-for-access-token)

Once you have the authorization code from the user in the redirect URI, request an access token by sending a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/token` with a Basic Authorization header.

Include the following required parameters either as query parameters or in the request body using the `x-www-form-urlencoded` format.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `authorization_code` |
| `code` | The `code` in the redirect URI after a successful user authorization. |
| `redirect_uri` | Your redirect URI. Use the same OAuth Redirect URL in your Marketplace app. |
| `state` | _(Optional)_ A string used to pass state between the request and callback. This can help prevent [cross-site request forgery](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6749#section-10.12). |

The Basic Authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret by a colon (`:`) and Base64 encoded. Use PKCE to enable user authorization with a public client ID an no client secret, without the need for a backend server. See [Using Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/#using-proof-key-for-code-exchange-pkce) for details.

#### Example request [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#example-request-1)

Copy

9

1

›

POST https://zoom.us/oauth/token?grant\_type=authorization\_code&code=Wk9PTV9BVVRIT1JJWkFUSU9OX0NPREU&redirect\_uri=https://example.com

Request headers

Copy

9

1

2

3

›

{

"Authorization":"Basic Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfSUQ6Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfU0VDUkVU"

}

If successful, the response body contains a JSON representation of the `access_token`.

Copy

2

8

{

"access\_token":"<JWT\_TOKEN>",

"token\_type":"bearer",

"refresh\_token":"<JWT\_TOKEN>",

"expires\_in":3600,

"scope":"user:read:user",

"api\_url":"https://api.zoom.us"

}

Access tokens expire after one hour. After your access token expires, you can follow the refresh flow to get a new one.

### App Type: [General](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-general-1)

Get an `access_token` from a device flow to call APIs on behalf of a Zoom user or Zoom account.

In your app build flow settings, navigate to **Features** \> **Embed** \> **Enable Meeting SDK** \> **Enable Use App on Device**.

To request a device code, user code, and verification URI, make a POST request with a basic authorization header to:

`https://zoom.us/oauth/devicecode?client_id=ZOOM_CLIENT_ID`

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

### Example request [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#example-request-2)

Copy

9

1

›

POST https://zoom.us/oauth/devicecode?client\_id=Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfSUQ

If successful, the response body is a JSON representation of the device code, user code, and verification URI.

"device\_code":"Wk9PTV9ERVZJQ0VfQ09ERQ",

"user\_code":"abcd1234",

"verification\_uri":"https://zoom.us/oauth\_device",

"verification\_uri\_complete":"https://zoom.us/oauth/device/complete/Wk9PTV9WRVJJRklDQVRJT05fVVJJX0NPTVBMRVRF",

"expires\_in":900,

"interval":5

}

Ask the user to navigate to the verification URI and display the user code. Alternatively, direct the user to the complete verification URI, which contains prefilled user code. Prompt the user to sign in if the user is not signed in to Zoom.

* * *

After entering the code, the user receives a prompt to allow the app. Once allowed, the app's landing page appears. The user receives a notification that the process can continue on the device.

You can now request an access token.

* * *

To request an access token, send a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/token` with a basic authorization header. Include the following required parameters either as query parameters or in the request body using the `x-www-form-urlencoded` format.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code` |
| `device_code` | The `device_code` returned in the previous step. |

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

### App Type: [General](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-general-2)

Get an `access_token` to send, edit, and delete Chatbot messages.

To install your Chatbot to your Zoom account, navigate to the **Local Test** page, and choose **Add App Now**.

You can also construct and navigate to the authorization URL yourself following this format:

Copy

9

1

›

https://zoom.us/oauth/authorize?response\_type=code&client\_id=ZOOM\_CLIENT\_ID&redirect\_uri=ZOOM\_REDIRECT\_URI

If this is the first time you are authorizing your app or if you have made webhook or scope changes, Zoom prompts you to authorize.

* * *

If authorized, you redirect to the `redirect_uri` with the authorization code in the code query parameter. You can use the `code` in the redirect URL for User Authorization OAuth to call additional API endpoints. If you only call Chatbot API endpoints, you do not need it.

Copy

9

https://example.com/?code=Wk9PTV9BVVRIT1JJWkFUSU9OX0NPREU

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `client_credentials` |

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

## Refresh an access token [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#refresh-an-access-token)

Here are the ways to refresh access tokens for these four authorization use cases.

Account authorization

User authorization

Device authorization

Client authorization

### App Type: [Server to Server](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/internal-apps/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-server-to-server-1)

Access tokens expire after one hour. After your access token expires, you can request a new one. Zoom does not require a separate refresh flow.

### App Type: [General](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-general-3)

Access tokens expire after one hour. After your access token expires, you can follow the refresh flow to get a new one.

To refresh an access token, send a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/token` with a basic authorization header. Include the following query parameters or provide them in the request body using the `x-www-form-urlencoded`format.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `refresh_token` |
| `refresh_token` | Your `refresh_token`. |

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

### Example request [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#example-request-5)

Copy

9

1

›

POST https://zoom.us/oauth/token?grant\_type=refresh\_token&refresh\_token=<JWT\_TOKEN>

Request headers

Copy

9

1

2

3

›

{

"Authorization":"Basic Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfSUQ6Wk9PTV9DTElFTlRfU0VDUkVU"

}

If successful, the response body is a JSON representation of the refreshed `access_token`.

Copy

9

1

2

3

4

5

6

7

8

›

{

"access\_token":"<JWT\_TOKEN>",

"token\_type":"bearer",

"refresh\_token":"<JWT\_TOKEN>",

"expires\_in":3600,

"scope":"user:read:user",

"api\_url":"https://api.zoom.us"

}

Refresh tokens expire after 90 days. You should always use the latest refresh token for the next refresh request. If your refresh token expires, you can direct the user to the authorize URL to restart the User OAuth flow.

### App Type: [General](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-general-4)

Access tokens expire after one hour. After your access token expires, you can follow the refresh flow to get a new one.

To refresh an access token, send a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/token` with a basic authorization header. Include the required parameters as query strings or in the request body using the `x-www-form-urlencoded` format.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `refresh_token` |
| `refresh_token` | Your `refresh_token`. |

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

## Revoke an access token [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#revoke-an-access-token)

### App Type: All [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-all)

To revoke an access token, send a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/revoke` with a basic authorization header. Include the required parameters as query strings or in the request body using the `x-www-form-urlencoded` format.

The basic authorization header is your Client ID and Client Secret with a colon `:` in between, Base64 Encoded.

## Me context [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#me-context)

You can replace the `userID` path parameter with `me` to target the user associated with the token. This approach lets you use user-specific endpoints without the need to look up or store the user ID for each token. For example:

| URL | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| `/v2/users/me` | `GET`, `PATCH` |
| `/v2/users/me/token` | `GET` |
| `/v2/users/me/meetings` | `GET`, `POST` |

## Deauthorization [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#deauthorization)

### App Type: [General](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/create/) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#app-type-general-6)

When a user deauthorizes or removes a **production** app, your app receives an HTTP POST request. The request goes to the deauthorization notification endpoint URL you specified on the App Listing page.

After receiving a [deauthorization webhook event](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/api/marketplace/events/#tag/app_deauthorized/POSTapp_deauthorized), apps must delete all associated user data.

An unsecured deauthorization notification endpoint URL leaves your server vulnerable to denial of service attacks. We recommend you verify the requests sent to your deauthorization notification endpoint URL with our [supported webhook verification methods](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/api/webhooks/#verify-webhook-events).

Below is an example deauthorization webhook event:

## Using Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#using-proof-key-for-code-exchange-pkce)

The **User Authorization** use case also supports [Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7636). Use PKCE when you don't have a backend server for user authorization, such as on mobile devices. Zoom offers a separate public client ID in the authorization request that doesn't require an associated client secret.

### Get your public client ID [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#get-your-public-client-id)

1. Open your app and navigate to **App Credentials** under **Basic Information**.
2. Toggle **Use Public Client OAuth** to on.
3. Copy the **public client ID** and send it, Base64 encoded, for user authorization. It does not require a client secret.

**Using with client ID and secret**

When you turn on public client OAuth, you can still use the `client ID:client secret` base64 encoded format with confidential client types.

### PKCE authorization flow [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#pkce-authorization-flow)

Generate a `code_verifier`, a cryptographically random string, locally in your client. Derive a `code_challenge` from it. For `S256`, take the SHA-256 hash of the `code_verifier` and Base64URL-encode it. Use your platform's crypto library, for example `CryptoKit` on iOS, `MessageDigest` on Android, or `crypto.subtle` in browsers.

Send the user to the authorization URL with your public client ID, `code_challenge`, and `code_challenge_method`:

Copy

9

1

›

https://zoom.us/oauth/authorize?response\_type=code&client\_id=ZOOM\_PUBLIC\_CLIENT\_ID&redirect\_uri=REDIRECT\_URI&code\_challenge=CODE\_CHALLENGE&code\_challenge\_method=S256

After the user clicks **Allow** on the consent screen, Zoom redirects to your `redirect_uri` with an authorization `code`.

To exchange the `code` for an access token, send a POST request to `https://zoom.us/oauth/token`. Unlike the confidential client flow, PKCE does not use an `Authorization` header. Send all fields in the request body as `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.

| Key | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `grant_type` | `authorization_code` |
| `code` | The authorization code from the redirect. |
| `client_id` | Your public client ID. |
| `redirect_uri` | The same redirect URI used in the authorization request. |
| `code_verifier` | The original `code_verifier`. |

If successful, the response body contains the `access_token`, `refresh_token`, and a `token_type` of `bearer`. You can now make authorized API requests.

### PKCE parameter reference [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#pkce-parameter-reference)

See the [Proof Key for Code Exchange by OAuth Public Clients](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7636) RFC for full details.

| Key | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `code_verifier` | A cryptographically random string generated locally by the client. Sent in the access token request so Zoom can validate the previously received `code_challenge`. |
| `code_challenge` | A challenge derived from the `code_verifier`. Sent in the authorization request. |
| `code_challenge_method` | The method used to derive the `code_challenge`, either `S256` or `plain`. Sent in the authorization request. Defaults to `plain` if not present. Public clients must use `S256`. |

### Detailed justification for PKCE [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#detailed-justification-for-pkce)

If you make your app public, you may need to add an explanation why your application requires a public client ID in production. This helps our application review team test your PKCE integration and confirm your intended OAuth flow. Indicate whether you plan to use:

- The confidential client OAuth flow (for example, a web app with a backend),
- The public client OAuth PKCE flow (for example, a mobile or desktop app), or
- Both.

This information ensures our security team can validate your configuration according to your intended use.

**Note**

The OAuth consent page must always be displayed for public clients that do not use a client secret ( [RFC 6819, Section 5.2.3.2 – Public Clients](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6819#section-5.2.3.2)). This prevents silent or automatic authorization that could expose user credentials or tokens to untrusted applications. This applies to the authorization code exchange step (`/oauth/token?grant_type=authorization_code`). It's not applicable to the refresh token flow.

### See also [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#see-also)

- [PKCE OAuth and the Meeting SDK for Android](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/meeting-sdk/android/start-join-mtg-webinar/pkce/)
- [Introducing PKCE support for public and confidential clients](https://developers.zoom.us/blog/public-pkce/) on the developer blog

## Supporting concurrent logins [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#supporting-concurrent-logins)

With confidential clients, a backend server can negotiate access tokens across multiple clients of the same end user account, if the developer wishes to support this concurrent client use case. When using a public client, there is no backend server to manage these tokens, since the clients communicate directly with the authentication APIs.

To address this use case, Zoom enables a feature called " **multi-auth token**" automatically when you enable a public client ID in the build flow. Multi-auth token mode allows any valid access token for the user to call Zoom APIs, not just the most recently-issued one.

## Using a loopback redirect URI [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#using-a-loopback-redirect-uri)

Native applications, desktop clients, CLI tools, and local development environments, can use a **loopback redirect URI** to receive the OAuth authorization response without exposing a publicly reachable endpoint. This approach follows the security recommendations in [RFC 8252, OAuth 2.0 for Native Apps](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8252).

**Note**

Loopback redirect is for **PKCE-enabled clients or native app clients**, not standard confidential OAuth clients.

With a loopback redirect, your application starts a temporary local HTTP server, directs the user's system browser to Zoom's authorization endpoint, and captures the authorization code when the browser redirects back to `http://127.0.0.1:{port}/{path}`. To implement, create the HTTP server first (e.g. on port `0`), read the assigned port, then open the browser.

### Eligibility [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#eligibility)

- **Use loopback for PKCE-enabled clients and native app clients.** Zoom matches loopback redirect URIs while ignoring only the port. The scheme, numeric loopback host, path, query, fragment, and user info must otherwise match the registered URI exactly.
- **Do not use loopback for simple OAuth apps that are not PKCE-enabled and native apps.** These must continue to use HTTPS redirect URIs. The user-facing error from the OAuth authorize endpoint is: `Invalid redirect: <redirectUri>.`

### When to use loopback redirection [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#when-to-use-loopback-redirection)

Use this method when your application runs locally on the user's machine and cannot receive inbound HTTPS callbacks from the internet. Common scenarios include:

- Desktop applications (Electron, native GUI apps)
- Command-line interface (CLI) tools
- Local development and testing environments

### Prerequisites [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#prerequisites)

- A registered Zoom Marketplace OAuth app.
- Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) enabled — required for all public/native clients.
- A loopback redirect URI registered in your app's OAuth allow list.

### Create a loopback redirect URI [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#create-a-loopback-redirect-uri)

1. **Generate a PKCE code verifier and challenge.** Create a cryptographically random `code_verifier` (43–128 characters) and derive the `code_challenge` using the S256 method.

2. **Start the local HTTP server** \- Bind to `127.0.0.1:0` to get an ephemeral port.

3. **Read the assigned port** \- Get the actual port from the server (e.g., `52936`). The port may vary on each run.

4. **Construct the redirect URI.** Build the URI using the loopback IP literal and the selected port:







Copy

























9



1







›













http://127.0.0.1:52936/callback

5. **Launch the system browser.** Open the user's default browser to Zoom's authorization endpoint with the required parameters:







Copy

5



6







›













https://zoom.us/oauth/authorize?response\_type=code



&client\_id=YOUR\_CLIENT\_ID



&redirect\_uri=http://127.0.0.1:52936/callback



&code\_challenge=YOUR\_CODE\_CHALLENGE



&code\_challenge\_method=S256



&state=YOUR\_RANDOM\_STATE

6. **Capture the redirect.** After the user authorizes, Zoom redirects the browser to your local listener. Extract the `code` and `state` query parameters from the incoming request.

7. **Validate the state parameter.** Confirm that the returned `state` matches the value you generated in step 4.

8. **Exchange the code for tokens.** Send a POST request to the token endpoint with the authorization code, redirect URI, and PKCE code verifier:

&client\_id=YOUR\_CLIENT\_ID



&code=AUTHORIZATION\_CODE



&redirect\_uri=http://127.0.0.1:52936/callback



&code\_verifier=YOUR\_CODE\_VERIFIER

9. **Shut down the listener.** Close the local HTTP server immediately after receiving the redirect.


### Register a loopback redirect URI [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#register-a-loopback-redirect-uri)

Register the loopback redirect URI with or without a port with the same scheme, numeric loopback host, and path your app will use (for example,`127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` are both supported for eligible clients, but they are matched as different hosts). Do not use `localhost`. Register and send numeric loopback literals. These formats are accepted for PKCE or native-style clients:

http://127.0.0.1

http://127.0.0.1:3000

http://127.0.0.1/callback

http://127.0.0.1:8080/callback

http://\[::1\]

http://\[::1\]:60123/callback

### Other considerations [\#](https://developers.zoom.us/docs/integrations/oauth/\#other-considerations)

- **Use**`127.0.0.1`, not `localhost`. The loopback IP literal avoids DNS resolution issues and prevents unintended network exposure. RFC 8252 explicitly recommends against using `localhost` for this reason.
- **Bind only to the loopback interface.** Never bind the listener to `0.0.0.0` or a public interface.
- **Close the listener immediately.** Shut down the local HTTP server as soon as you receive the authorization response to minimize the window of exposure.
- **Always use PKCE.** The code verifier and challenge mechanism prevents authorization code interception attacks, which are especially relevant for native apps where the client secret cannot be kept confidential.
- **Validate the**`state` parameter. Always compare the returned `state` to the value you generated to prevent CSRF attacks.
- **Handle port conflicts gracefully.** If the initially selected port becomes unavailable, retry with a different ephemeral port before presenting an error to the user. For example, port already in use errors, redirect URI mismatch errors (wrong host, wrong path), client not eligible for loopback (not PKCE-enabled), browser not opening or user closing browser before authorization.
- **Do not cache or reuse the listener port.** Select a fresh ephemeral port for each authorization attempt.
- **Rate limits.** There are no rate limits per loopback.
- **No maximum redirect attempts.** There is no explicit maximum number of redirect attempts before an authorization code expires.
